mercy_translation.text:
Once the human mind had fallen into sensible things, the Word submitted himself to appear through a body so that, as a human being, he might draw human beings to himself, turn their senses toward himself, and then, when they saw him as a human being, persuade them through the works he accomplished that he was not merely a human being but also God, the true Word and Wisdom of God.

Paul wishes to indicate this when he says: “Rooted and grounded in love, may you have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled with all the fullness of God.”

For the Word has stretched himself everywhere: above and below, into depth and breadth—above in creation, below in his becoming man, into the depth in Hades, and into the breadth throughout the world. All things have been filled with the knowledge of God.

For this reason, when he came, he did not immediately perform the sacrifice on behalf of all by handing his body over to death and raising it again, thereby making himself unseen. Rather, he also made himself visible through it, remaining in it and accomplishing such works and giving such signs as made him known no longer as a mere human being but as God the Word.

For through his becoming man the Savior acted in loving-kindness in both ways: he abolished death from us and renewed us; and although unseen and invisible, through his works he made himself manifest and made known that he is the Word of the Father, the Ruler and King of the universe.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The fourfold spatial imagery—height, depth, breadth, and what is below—is Athanasius' theological reading of Christ's universal work.
The text connects the Incarnation both with renewal from death and with revelation of the invisible Word.
